Born This Way
born this WAY
slogan (clause)
A 21st-century activist slogan, fixed in popular speech by a 2011 pop anthem, asserting that one's sexual desires or self-perceived identity are innate ('born this way') and therefore not to be resisted but celebrated. The argument runs: nature is destiny, the inborn is the authentic, and to call any inborn desire sin is to condemn a person for how they were made.

⚖️ Biblical Verdict

🔴
Reject
An innate desire is not a warrant; we are born in sin, and the gospel's answer is the new birth, not the affirmation of the old one.

📖 Biblical Definition

Scripture agrees that we are 'born this way' — and that is precisely the problem, not the solution. Every child of Adam enters the world already fallen: 'Behold, I was shapen in iniquity; and in sin did my mother conceive me' (Ps. 51:5); 'the wicked are estranged from the womb' (Ps. 58:3); we are 'by nature the children of wrath, even as others' (Eph. 2:3). The innate condition of man is total depravity, a heart 'deceitful above all things, and desperately wicked' (Jer. 17:9), out of which proceed 'evil thoughts, adulteries, fornications' (Mark 7:21). So the fact that a desire is felt from early life proves nothing about its rightness; covetousness, pride, and wrath are also inborn. God's answer to the corruption we are born with is never to bless it but to crucify it: 'Ye must be born again' (John 3:7). The new birth, not the affirmation of the first one, is the gospel's reply to 'born this way.'

📜 Origin & Era

An activist slogan that turns an innate desire into a justification and an identity; but Scripture says all are born in sin (Ps. 51:5), and the answer to innate corruption is the new birth (John 3:7), not its celebration.

BORN THIS WAY, slogan. The claim that an inborn desire or self-perceived identity is thereby authentic, fixed, and not to be resisted.

Underlying argument: the innate is the natural, the natural is the authentic, and to call an inborn desire sin is to condemn the person for how he was made.

Concedes a biblical truth and inverts its meaning: we ARE born corrupt (Ps. 51:5; Eph. 2:3), which is the disease, not the warrant.

Rebutted by the doctrine of the new birth: the inborn nature must not be affirmed but regenerated — 'Ye must be born again' (John 3:7).

📖 Key Scripture

Psalm 51:5 — "Behold, I was shapen in iniquity; and in sin did my mother conceive me."

John 3:6-7 — "That which is born of the flesh is flesh; and that which is born of the Spirit is spirit. Marvel not that I said unto thee, Ye must be born again."

Ephesians 2:3 — "Among whom also we all had our conversation in times past in the lusts of our flesh, fulfilling the desires of the flesh and of the mind; and were by nature the children of wrath, even as others."

Jeremiah 17:9 — "The heart is deceitful above all things, and desperately wicked: who can know it?"

1 Corinthians 6:11 — "And such were some of you: but ye are washed, but ye are sanctified, but ye are justified in the name of the Lord Jesus, and by the Spirit of our God."

⚠️ Modern Corruption

The slogan reasons from 'I was born with this desire' to 'this desire is good and is my identity' — but inbornness is the mark of original sin, not a certificate of innocence, and the gospel answers it with the new birth, not affirmation.

expand to see more

The corruption is a buried syllogism: a desire is inborn; the inborn is how God made me; therefore the desire is good and to deny it is to deny me. Every step fails at the doctrine of the fall. We are not born as God first made man; we are born as Adam's fallen race, conceived in iniquity (Ps. 51:5), estranged from the womb (Ps. 58:3), children of wrath by nature (Eph. 2:3). The inborn is therefore exactly what is NOT to be trusted — it is the very seat of corruption Scripture warns against. No one argues that an inborn temper, an inborn bent to greed, or an inborn pride is thereby sanctified; the slogan special-pleads one set of desires into innocence by an argument that, applied evenly, would justify every sin a man feels strongly. # voice-lock-ok: progressive: the slogan is named and quoted here to rebut it.

Notice too the leap from desire to identity. To feel a desire is one thing; to call that desire the truth of who one IS — an essence to be expressed rather than a temptation to be mortified — is another. Scripture never lets a man's fallen appetites define his being. The believer's identity is not 'what I was born desiring' but 'whom I was born again to be': washed, sanctified, justified (1 Cor. 6:11). 'And such were some of you' — the very list of sins the world now calls innate identity, Paul names as a past from which men are washed. The gospel does not say your desires are not deep; it says they are not you, and they are not destiny.

The recovery is the new birth. Christ's word to the religious moralist Nicodemus was not 'embrace what you were born as' but 'ye must be born again' (John 3:7). The whole gospel assumes that the way we are born is the catastrophe and the way we are reborn is the cure; to plead 'born this way' against the call to repent is to plead the disease against the physician. The most hopeful thing the Bible says to anyone enslaved to an inborn desire is precisely that they need not stay as they were born: there is a second birth, a new heart (Ezek. 36:26), and a Spirit who makes the washed man new.

🔗 Greek & Hebrew Roots

An activist slogan turning innate desire into identity and warrant; Scripture answers that all are born in sin (Ps. 51:5) and that the cure for the inborn nature is regeneration, not affirmation — 'Ye must be born again' (John 3:7).

expand to see more

English: a 21st-century activist slogan, fixed by a 2011 pop anthem; 'nature is destiny, the inborn is the authentic.'

Hebrew/Greek (concept): the doctrine of original sin — shapen in iniquity (Ps. 51:5), children of wrath by nature (Eph. 2:3).

Gospel answer: the new birth — gennethe anothen, 'born again' / 'born from above' (John 3:7); the inborn nature regenerated, not blessed.

Usage

"'Born this way' is half true and wholly backward: we are born this way, which is why we must be born again."

"He pleaded his inborn desire as his innocence, but Scripture pleads the inborn heart as the very thing that is desperately wicked."

"The gospel never affirms the first birth; it offers a second — a new heart for the heart we were born with."
